evidence.domain: Compared with 12 CFR 1024.17 and Appendix E (fetched). Matches: aggregate accounting trial balance, deposit and disbursement within the same month as in Appendix E, cushion cap at 1/6 of annual disbursements, low point = cushion, surplus >= $50 refund within 30 days only when current, shortage under one month's payment may be collected in 30 days. Departs: (1) deficiency is computed from the projected low point (neededZero - startBalance, calc.mjs:138) rather than as a negative account balance (1024.17(b)), so part of an ordinary shortage escapes the 12-month rule; (2) the deficiency branch ignores the under-one-month 30-day option in (f)(4)(i); (3) no reconciliation of the account history half of the annual statement (1024.17(i)(1)), stated as out of scope. An escrow analyst would raise (1) on the first statement with an early-year tax bill.

defects.what: Deficiency is computed as the shortfall below a zero projected low point (neededZero - startBalance) instead of a negative account balance (12 CFR 1024.17(b)). Any shortage whose low point dips below zero is partly relabelled a deficiency and the 12-month spread check is then skipped (calc.mjs:183 requires deficiencyCents === 0): start $500, $540 shortage collected over 6 months, which (f)(3)(ii) disallows, gives no finding.

Page defines a deficiency as 'a negative projected balance' / 'the balance would go negative' (FAQ and rules list), contrary to 1024.17(b), and tells users a deficiency 'may be repaid faster'; the headline promise to flag a shortage collected faster than allowed fails in exactly that case.
Tests pin the deficiency misreading as correct (start $0, Jan bill: deficiency 1100; $1,300 collected in one month 'not held to the 12-month rule'), and no test runs Appendix E.
Regulatory thresholds are unpinned: changing the $50 surplus threshold to $100, the 12-month spread limit to 8 months, or the one-month-payment boundary from >= to > leaves all 46 tests green.

'Most that is in question over a year' sums overlapping findings of different kinds: the payment excess x 12 already contains the servicer's higher bills and the cushion effect, which are added again (sample: 3,179.96 = 500 + 600 + 1,479.96 + 600).
Deficiency recovered in one payment is flagged even when it is under one month's payment, which 1024.17(f)(4)(i)(B) allows within 30 days (info severity only).
Bill-entry note contradicts itself: 'the full year's bill, not one installment' followed by 'enter a tax paid in two installments as one row per installment'.

verdict: The aggregate-accounting arithmetic is exact: the CFPB's own Appendix E example reproduces to the dollar in every month of Step 2 and Step 3 (monthly 130, cushion 260, start balance 1040, low point 260 in December), and the $50 surplus and under-one-payment 30-day rules hold at their boundaries. But the tool defines a deficiency by the projected low point rather than by a negative account balance as 12 CFR 1024.17(b) does, and it then switches off the 12-month shortage-spread check, so a $540 shortage from a $500 balance collected over 6 months goes unflagged. That is the case a homeowner with a large insurance jump most needs. The page's FAQ repeats the wrong definition, the tests pin it, three of five seeded threshold mutants survive, and the 'most in question' total double-counts overlapping findings. Below the bar on correctness, claims and verification; the fix (deficiency = max(0, -startBalance), an Appendix E test, boundary tests for $50, 12 months and one month's payment) is small.
